ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Neurology (peripheral nerve) Consultation — Roald Amundsen — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: Two-week follow-up and neurology consultation with nerve conduction studies

text.paragraph: Cold-induced burning pain, numbness and color change in the fingers of both hands for many winters, worse this winter, in a 55-year-old polar explorer with frostbite of the fingers in early adulthood. Please confirm or exclude a late post-frostbite neuropathy, nerve entrapment, or another polyneuropathy, and advise on treatment that will not make him drowsy, as he drives and flies. [S]
Urgency: Within two weeks, with nerve conduction studies. [S]

list.item: Is this a late neuropathy from his old frostbite, or is there an entrapment or another cause?
Are nerve conduction studies or other tests needed?
What treatment do you recommend, given that he wishes to avoid drowsiness and, at first, tablets?
How should the cold-induced color change be managed?
How can he protect his fingers if he works in the cold again?

text.paragraph: Mr. Amundsen, a 55-year-old polar explorer, is seen at the request of Dr. Solheim-Achebe for burning pain and numbness in the fingers of both hands brought on by cold. The attacks have come every winter for many years and have been worse this winter, lasting up to an hour after he comes indoors, with the fingers turning white, then blue, then red. Between attacks the fingertips are slightly numb. There is no weakness, clumsiness apart from the cold, foot symptoms, neck pain, or night-time tingling that wakes him in warm weather. He had frostbite of the fingers of both hands in his early twenties. He has never smoked, drinks rarely, and takes no regular medicines. He drives, flies as a passenger and navigator, and would rather avoid tablets, and certainly any that make him drowsy. [S]
Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Roald Engelbregt Gravning Amundsen was born on July 16, 1872, at the farm Hvidtsten in Borge, Østfold, Norway. [D]

He wrote that as a young man he was near-sighted, a defect that had gradually improved but was not wholly corrected, and that he had refused to wear the glasses prescribed for him so that it would not keep him out of military training. [D]

On a winter ski crossing of the Hardangervidda plateau in his early twenties he nearly died in a snow cave during a rest stop, and he wrote that he and his companion both got their fingers badly frostbitten while breaking into a nailed-up hut. [D]

As first mate of the Belgian Antarctic expedition in the Belgica (1897 to 1899), he spent thirteen months in the pack ice. He wrote that every member of the ship's company was afflicted with scurvy and all but three were prostrated by it; once fresh seal and penguin meat was eaten, the men plainly improved within a week. The expedition's physician had encouraged the crew to eat seal and penguin. [D]

A physician historian argues that the heart failure seen on the Belgica expedition, described at the time as 'polar anaemia', was almost certainly wet beriberi from thiamine deficiency, and that most sufferers were probably also deficient in vitamin C. [R]

He led the first voyage through the Northwest Passage in a single ship, the Gjøa (1903 to 1906), and on December 14, 1911, he and four companions were the first to reach the South Pole. In 1925 he led a flight by flying boat toward the North Pole from Ny-Ålesund, and in 1926 the flight of the airship Norge across the Arctic. [D]

On the Maud expedition, in the autumn of 1918, he fell down the ship's runway onto his right shoulder; the fracture was set aboard by a crewman trained in first aid, and he kept to his bed for eight days. On November 8, 1918, a polar bear struck him on the back, leaving minor gashes. He wrote that he could not at first lift his right hand to use a pencil, worked the arm daily for months, and that a surgeon in Seattle who X-rayed it in 1921 found the shoulder in a condition that theoretically would make the arm unusable. [D]

About the New Year of 1918 to 1919, working in the small, unventilated observatory of the Maud with a kerosene vapour lamp, he became drowsy, felt his heart beating unnaturally, and nearly lost consciousness before he reached fresh air. He wrote that the violent palpitation lasted several days, that for months strenuous exercise set his heart pounding, and that in February he was exhausted by climbing a fifty-foot hill. [D]

He wrote that in February 1922 a heart specialist in London told him "No more expeditions!" and to avoid all strenuous exercise; nine months later he travelled about 800 miles on foot through the snow from Point Barrow to Nome, and five years later he wrote that he had had no unpleasant results from his exertions. [D]
The Norwegian encyclopedia describes the observatory episode as carbon monoxide poisoning. [R]

He bought the house Uranienborg at Svartskog, on the Bunnefjord near Oslo, in 1908 and lived there for twenty years. His study had an exercise spring installed in the floor for his strength training, and a pump brought salt water from the fjord for his morning bath. [D]
After his 1927 lecture tour of Japan he returned by the Trans-Siberian railway; letters place him in Oslo in August 1927 and again in May 1928. [D]

The Norwegian encyclopedia writes that by the end of his career he felt tired, lonely and bitter; he was 55, with persistent money problems and no more poles to conquer. He had declared himself personally bankrupt. [D]

Cold-induced neuropathic pain and cold sensitivity of the fingers of both hands, a late sequela of frostbite in early adulthood: small-fiber pattern with normal nerve conduction studies, cold allodynia and reduced pinprick at the fingertips, and cold-induced vasospasm

text.paragraph: Vital signs recorded on 1928-02-24; see the referring visit's Vital Signs section. [S]

tr.td: Fingertips cool with slightly delayed capillary refill; no ulcers, pitting or scars; normal radial and ulnar pulses
Reduced pinprick and cold sensation at the tips of the index to little fingers of both hands; cold allodynia on a cold tuning fork; vibration and joint position normal
Normal bulk and strength in both hands, including thumb abduction and finger abduction; reflexes normal and symmetric
Tinel sign at wrist and elbow and Phalen test negative on both sides

text.paragraph: No results recorded at this visit.

list.item: Post-frostbite small-fiber neuropathy and cold-induced vasospasm of the fingers (M79.2). The history of frostbite, the fingertip distribution, the loss of pinprick and cold sensation with cold allodynia, the normal large-fiber function, and the cold-induced color change fit a late small-fiber neuropathy with vasospasm after frostbite, which is recognized as a long-term consequence. Normal nerve conduction studies exclude carpal and cubital tunnel syndromes and a large-fiber polyneuropathy, and the blood tests exclude diabetes, B12 deficiency, thyroid disease and kidney disease. No further tests are needed. Skin biopsy for small-fiber density would not change management. [S]

Treatment. He wishes to avoid oral treatment, and the pain is localized to the fingers, so capsaicin cream is reasonable first under NICE CG173. If it is not enough, duloxetine is the best of the first-line oral drugs for him, because amitriptyline, gabapentin and pregabalin are more likely to cause drowsiness; tramadol should be avoided, both because it is not for long-term use and because it interacts with duloxetine. [S]

Cold-induced vasospasm. Secondary to the old cold injury. No ulcers or signs of critical ischemia. Cold protection is the main treatment; a calcium-channel blocker would be considered only if attacks remained frequent and severe despite it. [S]

text.paragraph: Data reviewed: Dr. Solheim-Achebe's intake note and blood tests: HbA1c 5.4%, fasting glucose 94 mg/dL, vitamin B12 512 pg/mL, TSH 1.8 mIU/L, creatinine 0.96 mg/dL, ALT 24 U/L, hemoglobin 14.9 g/dL. Nerve conduction studies today: median, ulnar and radial sensory and motor conduction normal in both arms, with normal distal latencies and no slowing across the elbow; median-ulnar palmar comparison normal; digital sensory responses low-normal and symmetric. [S]

list.item: Capsaicin 0.075% cream to the painful fingers four times a day, washing the hands after use; it may sting for the first week. [S]

If pain remains troublesome after four weeks, duloxetine 30 mg daily for a week, then 60 mg daily, with review of pain, adverse effects, mood, sleep and blood pressure, a sodium and liver enzyme check in the first weeks, no tramadol, and no abrupt stopping. [S]
Cold protection: liner gloves under mittens, heated gloves and hand warmers, warming the hands before fine work, no cold-water hand washing, and checking the skin for injury. [S]
No calcium-channel blocker for now; reconsider if attacks of vasospasm stay frequent and severe. [S]
Previously frostbitten fingers are more vulnerable to cold injury: in cold work, extra insulation, frequent checks, and early rewarming. [S]
No further tests; neurology review only if weakness, spreading sensory loss, or ulceration develops. [S]
Discussed with Dr. Solheim-Achebe, who saw him the same day. The results and options were explained to Mr. Amundsen, who chose to start with the cream and agreed with the plan. [S]
Follow-up: Neurology review on request; primary care review in four weeks. [S]
